# Finetuner

> Reward hacking, long-horizon agent trajectory evaluation, and the open problems in coding-agent post-training.

## The open problems

- Training graders to improve performance on coding tasks with non-verifiable reward. Classical tests, rubrics, and agentic graders all get hacked by RL agents. Reward hacking is actively anticipated; reward design is the bottleneck, not reward compute.
- Dense reward signals on step transitions, not just whole-trajectory outcomes. RL environment, reward, post-train data, and long-context eval pipeline are today all four immature for long-horizon tool-using agents.
- Agent-trajectory data — browser, GUI, SWE code traces — has no canonical format or pipeline. Browser interactions, SWE/code traces, GUI sessions, and multi-turn workflows are the unsolved data surface.
- Real-usage feedback loops don't exist. Quality is not yet measurable or operational. Agent failure taxonomy is open. Quality metric definitions are ambiguous.
- Standards for data quality and reproducibility across large-scale agent gyms — coverage metrics, invariance checks, trace audits — do not yet exist. Keeping training signals faithful, stable, and scalable is open.
- Session-level good, bad, and degraded session primitives, alerting, and triage for making quality measurable and operational at the training loop.
- No standardized way to compare rubric methodologies across domains. Reward-signal iteration is measured in days of manual experimentation. Reward hacking is a recurring, ongoing failure mode that needs dedicated detection, not one-off mitigation. Human-feedback-data quality assessment is still manual and ad-hoc.
- Reward hacking, mode collapse, and exploitable loopholes.
- Reward design, trajectory evaluation, interruption handling, observation and state design, tool and action interface design, and curriculum learning are open problems. Long-horizon agent trajectory evaluation lacks an industry-standard method. Agent trajectory and long-horizon eval is an open research problem.

## Key topics

- non-verifiable reward in coding-agent training
- reward hacking, mode collapse, exploitable loopholes
- long-horizon agent trajectory evaluation methods
- dense reward signals on step transitions
- agent trajectory data format standardization (browser, GUI, SWE traces)
- real-usage feedback loops for AI agents
- agent gym data quality standards and reproducibility
- session-level quality metrics for monitoring AI agents
- agent failure taxonomy and quality metric definitions
- reward-signal iteration as a manual multi-day bottleneck
- rubric methodology comparison across domains
- preference model human data experiments around reward hacks
- RLHF data labeling quality control
- curriculum learning, interruption handling, observation and state design, tool and action interface design as open problems
- coverage metrics, invariance checks, trace audits
